title: A full screen takes the keyboard down with it
body: Chris, Sep 26: "if I ever open a full screen, I need the keyboard to go away automatically." He was typing, opened a diagram full screen, and the keyboard stayed up over the bottom third of it. Now any full screen drops the keyboard as it opens: a reply the agent opens on its own, a pill in the chat, a deck, a plan, a picture, the camera. Closing it leaves the keyboard down, and what you typed is still in the field. A new test types in the chat, opens a full screen and checks the keyboard is gone. It rides the next release.
short: Opening anything full screen puts the keyboard away, and closing it keeps it down.

title: Yui holds less in memory, and a test checks it before every release
body: Chris, Sep 25: "I think there must be memory leakage all over the place." We measured first. A scripted session on the simulator opens five agents with 486-message threads, galleries, decks, games and screens 2 to 12, goes full screen, then idles, while the app logs its memory every second and a leak checker runs at the start and the end. The big leak was the deck you swipe inside a message: every one that scrolled out of the thread left its pages behind, about 1,550 leaked objects over one session. It pages with a plain scroll now, and the session ends with zero new leaks. Pictures used to decode at full size for as long as their message lived; now each is decoded at the size it is drawn and shares one cache with a size limit that empties when the phone runs low. Videos let go of their player when they leave the screen, a long thread drops the older rows it drew once you are back at the bottom, and a few lists that only ever grew are gone or trimmed. The session's peak fell from 243 MB to 203 MB and launch from 137 MB to 124 MB, with taps and scrolling as fast as before. The same session now runs before every release and fails on new leaks, growth or a peak over 300 MB. It rides the next release.
short: Yui uses less memory: peak down from 243 to 203 MB in a long session, and no new leaks.

title: A timeline opened on its own sits at the top
body: A saved screen holding only a timeline, opened full screen from the shelf, used to spread three rows over the whole phone: big empty gaps, and the running row's highlight about 400 points tall. The rows' dot column was flexible, so they soaked up the extra height the full screen hands its content. Now each row keeps its natural height and a timeline starts at the top, like a page you read down. A card, timer or stat alone still sits in the middle. The folded 'earlier' button's line was fixed the same way. It rides the next release.
short: A timeline opened full screen keeps its rows tight and starts at the top.

title: Agent tables in the Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers
body: The web half of step 2 for agent tables. The Python, Kotlin and Rust parsers now read table create, put and query, and each carries its own copy of the store: upsert by key, rows that append with no key, today and now dates, where filters, sort with empty cells last, group and totals. title: Talk about a setting, built: change your agent by talking
body: Step 2 of 2. Every item in Controls (the personality, a memory, a skill, a schedule, and the model card, read only) now has a Talk about this button. It closes the drawer and pins the item above the composer as a chip: tap it to see the item, x to take it off, and a second item replaces the first. Say what you want and your message goes out with a short line naming the item, never its text. Your Mac puts the item into the agent's turn itself, with any line holding a key hidden. The agent proposes, it never writes: your Mac checks the change with the same rules as a hand edit and draws it in the chat as a before and after, with Apply and Keep it as is. Apply writes it with no agent turn, keeps the old copy and logs it, and a card says it is done. If the file changed on your Mac meanwhile, nothing is written and Ask again gets a fresh proposal. A memory with a key in it can be talked about but never changed from the phone. Only the owner can do any of this. Tested end to end on the simulator over the live relay: a new line in SOUL.md, one Keep it as is, a terminal edit mid-proposal, a memory forgotten, a schedule moved to 7:30, and nothing key-shaped in the messages. Rides the next release.

title: Taps answer at once, and a long thread scrolls smooth
body: Chris, Sep 25: "I am not getting ultra smoothness when I click around. Things feel delayed. Very efficient like Telegram." We measured first, on a 500-message thread in the simulator. Opening it took over three seconds, a tap on a choice took more than a second to show, and every change to the thread redrew all 500 rows. The fixes: each row now knows when it hasn't changed and skips its redraw; what the thread reads on every pass (which rows show, which bubble wears the reaction, the pages) is worked out once per change instead of once per row; markdown is parsed once per message; a long thread draws its newest 60 rows and adds more as you scroll up; and dragging the drawer only redraws the drawer. The look is the same, light and dark. Warm thread open went from about 3 s to under 350 ms, a choice tap from 1.4 s to 58 ms, a reaction from 300 ms to 29 ms, a sent bubble from 2.4 s to 145 ms, and scroll hitches from 63 to under 2 ms per second. Real phone numbers come in through the app's own perf log once the build is out. Rides the next build.
short: Thread open 3 s to under 350 ms, taps under 100 ms, scroll hitches near zero. Same look.

title: The MCP server and Telegram read Yui Lines like the app again
body: Two copies of the Yui Lines parser had gone quietly stale. The MCP server that lets Claude, ChatGPT and other MCP hosts put screens on your phone, and the Telegram renderer, each carry a copy of the site's parser. When agent tables and app restyles arrived, the parser split into three files, but the scripts that copy it still took one. So the MCP server refused query, put, theme app and the new shapes diagrams as unknown lines, and Telegram pushed them all behind Open in Yui. Both copy scripts now follow the parser's imports and bring the whole set, so the next file it grows comes along on its own. The MCP server is redeployed and its live test, 106 of 106 checks, now sends a theme app, a table, a put, a query and a shapes diagram in one screen and sees them accepted. Telegram draws a shapes diagram as words: the title, the labels in order with arrows between them, and the caption. A query opens in Yui, since the tables live on the phone, and table and put lines send nothing. 73 of 73 Telegram checks. Nothing changes in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/telegram.

If the agent stops passing the safe-to-share rules it reads Paused by its owner, and messages wait. On your side, every agent's settings now say Safe to share, or Not safe to share and why, in plain words: it has a shell on your computer. Inviting someone is one screen from Yui: who, which safe agents, the look, what each says first, and whether to keep it as a template; Invite runs the scripts and hands back the link. Taking an agent back sends their phone a silent push, so it leaves the list at once; if the thread was open it closes with Basil is no longer shared with you. Thirty days later the old thread is deleted. Two gaps closed too: photos now work both ways in a shared thread, each kept in that person's own folder, and replies are fitted to the client's own phone, not yours. Rides the next build.

title: Yui now times itself: speed numbers from real phones, every day
body: The speed budget written earlier today is now measured. On the phone, nine moments are timed from your tap to the frame that shows the answer: a key appearing, your bubble after Send, an agent's message landing, a page swipe settling, full screen opening, a thread opening (first and later), launch and coming back. Each shows by name in Instruments and is timed on the phone's own clock. Memory is sampled every 30 seconds, and Apple's daily MetricKit report adds hangs, scroll hitches, memory peaks and crash stacks. It all travels as numbers only: no message text, no names, nothing you wrote. A new table, yui_perf, keeps each person's rows to themselves and their own agents, at most 500 a day, gone after 90 days. Yui (the agent) reads them into a daily report: p50 and p95 against the budget, what got slower than the build before, and the worst hang stacks, matched to code. The war room has a Speed panel under Builds (the shot uses sample numbers until real ones come in), and the morning briefing gets one line only when something got worse. Test builds have a Speed switch in Settings that shows the last keystroke time and the frame rate. What the build taught is in section 10 of the speed budget. Rides the next build.

title: Ask any agent to restyle Yui, in the app

title: Share an agent with a client, and take it back
body: The plumbing for sharing is live. You pick agents for an invite, each in a look and with a first message. The person signs in and the agent is in their list, dressed the way you picked, its first message waiting. Each person gets their own thread, and you never read it; neither does anyone else you invite. Take the agent back and it is gone from their app on the next open, and the agent can no longer read or write that thread. Safety is checked three times. The agent's computer reports how it is set up with every heartbeat, and only an agent with no shell, no files, no reach into the rest of the computer, no shared memory and a model reached through an API counts as safe to share. The grant script refuses anything else and says which rule failed, the database refuses it again, and the agent checks itself before every turn for someone who is not its owner. Tested on the simulator with a made-up client: Penny shows up in pink, says hi, and after a revoke she is gone. Next in the app: the invite screen for you, and a Shared by line for them.

title: Invite a client and their agents are already there, on paper and in the playground
body: Invites are how new people get into Yui right now. This step writes down what an invite can carry: a set of agents, each in a look you pick, each with a first message. The person signs in with Apple and their agent list is already filled, with a new message waiting from each one. They get their own thread with each agent. They can mute one or move it in the list, but not rename it or delete it. Take an agent back and it leaves their app at once. The harder part is safety. Most agents on a developer's computer can run any command and read any file, which is fine for their owner and never fine for someone else. So an agent can be shared only if it passes five rules: its own profile, no shell and no files outside a sandbox, no reach into the rest of the computer, nothing carried from one person to the next, and a model reached through an API. The grant script refuses any other agent, the database refuses it again, and the agent checks itself before every turn for someone who is not its owner. Try both sides in the playground: making the invite, and the first open. The app gets it in a later release.

title: Group threads: the plumbing is live
body: Yesterday we wrote down how a group of agents should behave. Today the database and the agent side do it. A group has its own thread, with a lead who answers anything you don't address. Your message goes to the agents you @, and only to them; the others see it on their next turn. When one agent @s another, the ask goes through on a budget: three handoffs and eight agent turns per message by default. Past that the ask is held until you say Let it or Stop, and Stop also cancels every handoff nobody has picked up yet. Each agent still reads only its own messages. What it knows of the rest of the group is a short quote above each ask and one line per message since its last turn, and only while it is a member. The agents' guide got a Groups section: answer only your part, hand work on in one plain sentence, never bounce it back. We tested it on three new cases and it passed all three. The database side passed 69 checks against the live project. The app's side, the New group sheet and the thread itself, is next and ships in a later release.
short: Group threads work under the hood: who answers, handoffs on a budget, Let it and Stop. The app is next.

title: Group threads: several agents in one conversation, on paper and in the playground

The rule for who answers is simple: the agent you @ answers, and if you @ nobody, the group's lead does. Nobody jumps in on a message that wasn't for them. When one agent asks another for help, the thread shows it as its own row, both faces and the ask, and every agent keeps its own colors. Agents can keep handing work on, but on a budget: one message of yours buys a few handoffs and at most eight agent turns. Past that, the ask waits for you with two buttons, Let it and Stop here, and a Stop button sits on the working rows the whole time. The spec also covers how a group is stored, why no agent can read another agent's messages even in a group, and what older copies of the app see. Try the mock in the playground: Coach plans race week, asks Sage for a wind-down, and Sage's ask to Quill hits the guard. The app gets it in a later release.

title: Connect your tools: the plan, and a flow you can try
body: Agents get useful when they can reach your calendar, your mail and your CRM. This step writes down how that will work in Yui, and turns the connect screens into a flow you can run. A connector is the tool's own MCP server, the open standard agents use to call tools: Google now runs one for Calendar and one for Gmail, and HubSpot runs one too. You sign in once, on Google's or HubSpot's own page, never in Yui. Before that, each tool gets a consent step that says what it allows in plain words instead of scope names: Calendar can see your events and find a time, and adding one is a separate ask later; Gmail can read, label and write drafts, and has no send button, so every draft waits for you; HubSpot sees only what your own login can see. The sign-in stays with your agent on your own computer, never in the app and never in a Yui database, and you can switch a tool off from the drawer or on Google and HubSpot directly. The sign-in buttons come from the agent after the flow, because a real sign-in link is made fresh for each person. Nothing signs in yet: the buttons open the spec. Real sign-in is step 2, and it needs a Google Cloud project and a HubSpot app registered first. Try it in the playground under Flow: connect your tools, and read it at /developers/connectors.

title: Agents keep data on your phone: tables
body: An agent can now keep a workout log, today's macros or a small CRM, and draw it any time. Three new words in Yui Lines do it. table create makes a table with typed columns (text, number, date, on or off). put writes one row: with a key it updates that row, without one it adds a row, so a log just appends. query draws the rows as a table, a list, a chart or one big number, and it stays live: send a put and every view on screen redraws. A query can filter (Day=today), sort, and total by group, so "best set per lift" or "protein by day" is one line. Dates like today and today-7 are read on the phone, so the agent never has to know yours. The rows stay on the phone. The agent sees them only when you tick a box in a list or tap Send on the rows you choose to share. This step is the spec and the web version: try the three starters in the playground under Agent tables, send the put in the agent line and watch the views change. Rows you add stay in your browser until you reset them. The iPhone app gets the same store next.

title: Cron failures go to Yui, not to your chat
body: Chris sent a screenshot of his Yui thread: a raw alert that a weekly job had failed, with a Python traceback in it. He did not want those. There is nothing for him to do with one, and it would come back to Yui anyway. So now every scheduled job Yui runs without an agent goes through a small guard script. When the job works, its message goes out exactly as before. When it fails or runs too long, the guard says nothing in the chat. It logs the failure, and it opens one card on Yui's board for that job, or adds a note to the card that is already open. Yui's lane driver reads that log every half hour and fixes the script or hands it to whoever owns the broken part. Chris hears about it only when the same job has failed three runs in a row and it is holding up Yui work, as one short line, never a traceback. The failing job itself, a weekly report that crashed on an older Python, was fixed first. A script on the Mac, so nothing to screenshot.

title: Week of Sep 21: from a first build to build 96, then a pause for 0.2.0
body: Yui's first week in public. On Monday there was a pitch and a roadmap. The first TestFlight build went out Wednesday, and by Friday the app had reached build 96: Sign in with Apple, every preset drawn native, decks and full-screen plans, reactions, replies, @mentions, slash commands, games, a war room with a timeline you can reorder, and a drawer for each agent. Agents from outside Hermes can talk in Yui now: Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, LangGraph, CrewAI, n8n and any A2A agent. The site grew a public board, a changelog by build, See it, the library and Thoughts. The honest problem: we shipped too often. Five uploads in one day, and Apple started turning builds away. So TestFlight is paused except for crash fixes, and the next build will be one real release, 0.2.0, with the drawer as each agent's home and screens that refresh in place. After that, the MVP test: a stranger goes from invite to first screen with no help.

title: Screens your Yui can't draw yet turn into words

body: Chris wants Yui on the Mac too. It is now a written plan anyone can pick up. title: Asks sit with what they ask about
body: Chris's feedback on the war room: every ask was two cards, the context on top and the buttons in a separate box under it, so the answer looked cut off from what it was about. Now each ask is one card: the card's tag, its name and the context, then the question and the buttons. Two answers ride every ask, always last. Not yet is for when the ask assumes you already did something, like a browser step. The card stays waiting and nothing restarts. You decide hands the call back, and the agent picks the option it recommends and goes. Under the hood, choose and pick take tag, title and body, in the app, on the web and in the MCP App. Phones on an older build still get the two-card layout until the next build.

title: Flows, written in Mermaid
body: Plan mode walks you through a few screens in a straight line. Flows add the map. A flow is a Mermaid flowchart, the same text GitHub draws as a chart: each box carries one screen, and the labels on the arrows are conditions on your earlier answers. Pick Shop and the intake asks about products and payments; pick Landing page and it skips the page list. The same step reads 4 of 9 on one branch and 4 of 6 on the other. Back walks the path you took, the review lists only what you answered on it, and the agent gets one event with the answers and the path. An agent can send a flow inline or run a saved one by name, like flow website-intake. Three starter flows come from real work: a client website intake, scoping a project yourself, and a workout check-in. All three run in the playground, and a browser test takes every branch of every one. This step is the spec and the web runtime; the app runs flows next. Spec: /developers/flows.

title: The admin console, scoped
body: Yui will need people who run it from the top, so we wrote down who they are before building anything. Five roles: the owner, a super user or two, admins for the daily work, support who can look things up but change nothing alone, and a company's own admin who runs only their people and their default agents. A table says what each role can touch: invites, accounts, the kill switch and limits, feature flags, announcements, feedback, usage numbers and an audit log. Next to each control is what exists today and what is missing. Our recommendation is an Admin section inside the app, not a web console: Sign in with Apple already works there, and the site has no login to secure. A role is a row checked on every request, never inside the token, and anything destructive asks again with Face ID and a fresh Apple sign-in. Admins never read messages: the admin API has no way to return them, and the doc lists exactly what is visible. It ends with three phases and six cards to pick from. No build yet, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/admin.

title: The app draws
body: Feedback on build 96 asked Yui to draw a little window with some things crossed out and others highlighted, instead of explaining in words. The app now draws sketches itself. An agent sends a frame, a window, a phone or a chat bubble, and a few rows: some struck out, some highlighted, some greyed, some drawn as buttons, blank ones as filler, each with an optional short note and an arrow. One line splits it into a before and an after. In the chat a sketch sits on a card. On a full-screen page it is the page's picture: the frame comes on first, then each row, then the headline and the words. A sketch with no page before it is a page that is only the drawing. The spec gained that rule, so agents can put a sketch right under a page line, and all five parsers and the web playground follow it. VoiceOver reads each drawn row with its marks, so a crossed-out line is read as crossed out. Lands with the next build.

title: Yui Lines in Rust
body: Yui Lines now has a fifth parser, in Rust. It is a crate with no dependencies: no regex library and no serde, only the standard library, with a small JSON reader of its own for custom lines. Each rule of the JavaScript parser is ported line by line, with the pattern it replaces written next to it. It passes all 445 shared test vectors in 25 files, read straight from the spec folder, and spec/conformance/run-all.sh now runs it next to JavaScript, Python and Kotlin. We also fed it 35,000 random documents and compared every result with the JavaScript parser: whole parses, streams cut into random chunks, what opens full screen, which pages can talk, and every screen with its defaults filled in. No differences. The README lists the few Unicode edge cases Rust strings cannot hold. The Developers page lists all five parsers. Go or C# is a good first contribution.

title: AG-UI agents in Yui
body: Agents served over AG-UI can come into Yui by their URL. AG-UI is the protocol agents use to talk to the app in front of them, and Microsoft Agent Framework, CopilotKit, Mastra and Pydantic AI all speak it. The new bridge makes Yui that app. Each message you send is one run, and the bridge keeps the conversation, since AG-UI servers remember nothing between runs. Screens are a tool the agent calls, yui_show: the run stops there, the screen goes to your phone, and your tap goes back as the tool's answer. That is AG-UI's own way of waiting on a person, so nothing is bent to fit. We ran Agent Framework's own AG-UI endpoint on a small local model, with instructions that never mention Yui, through live Yui on a test account: asked for a drink, it called yui_show with a Tea or Coffee picker on the first try, took the tap back, remembered it the next turn, and a crash in the middle of a turn still got one answer, 16 of 16 checks. The bridge reuses the A2A bridge's Yui side, so delivery works the same. One open question for Chris: whether Yui should also read A2UI, Google's UI format, which Agent Framework can send over AG-UI. Our take is not now. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/agui.

title: Full-screen pages tell a story
body: Feedback on build 96 held up a long answer read as pages: a card inside the full screen, a title cut off at "with the…", and a bullet list split across three pages. Now full screen is the whole stage. There is no card on it. Each page carries one idea: every list item gets its own page, and prose comes a sentence or two at a time. The headline is set big and sized to its words, so a five-word idea fills the screen, and it never breaks a word. The body is a second, quieter voice. A thin bar per page runs across the top. Words spring on when a page arrives and drift off when it leaves; with Reduce Motion they only fade. Titles stop after a whole clause, and a lead-in that ends in a colon ends in "…" so the next page picks it up. Decks, plans and walkthroughs all open this way, and host reports no longer repeat a title with "(2/3)". Each page leaves room for a picture. Drawn ones come next. Lands with the next build.

title: Agents can draw now
body: From TestFlight feedback: "Yui should be pretty good at just drawing different stuff so we don't even have to generate images or screenshots." One line in the middle splits it into before and after. It sends nothing back; it is there to show instead of tell. Agents learn it in channel guide v18, next to long reports. title: Yui's values, written down
body: Feedback on a build-ready deck said it plainly: three cards of split-up text is not what Yui is. The same note named what Yui should be, and those are now eight values on one page: screens, not text bombs; one idea per page; type tells the story; full screen is the whole stage, with no card inside it; draw it, don't describe it; say what is being done, not who did it; nothing cut off mid-sentence; every button does something. Each comes with one example. The agent guide points to them where it teaches long answers, and the build-in-public rules hold progress entries and Thoughts to them. The app work they call for (full-screen pages that tell a story, little drawn windows) is on the board next. Page: /developers/values.

title: Flue agents in Yui
body: Agents built with Flue, the TypeScript agent framework from the team behind Astro, can come into Yui. Flue adds integrations as channels: you run `flue add channel` and hand the guide it prints to your coding agent. Yui now has that guide, plus a small connector. Your Flue app dials out to Yui, so there is no webhook to expose, and every message you send goes to the agent through Flue's own dispatch. Its answer comes back once, even across a crash. Yui's agent guide goes into the agent's instructions, and that is all it takes to get screens. We ran a Flue agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker its own instructions never asked for, answered the tap, remembered it the next turn, and a crash in the middle of a turn still got one answer, 14 of 14 checks. The connector's Yui side is the same code the A2A bridge runs, now shared. On Cloudflare, where Flue agents usually live, Yui will push turns to the app instead; that waits on the hosted connector. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/adapters.

title: Chat with a screen
short: An agent can keep the composer on one of its screens, so you can type about what is there without going back to the chat.
body: Screens beside the chat are full screen, for reading and tapping, and typing happens in the chat. Now an agent can open a screen up for talk: one line, `>2 talk`, keeps the composer on screen 2. The field says "About screen 2", and what you type there reaches the agent with a first line that names the screen, so it knows you mean the plan on it and can change it in place. Your message shows in the chat with a small "From screen 2" mark that takes you back. `talk off` closes it again, and clearing the screen closes it too. Screens without it stay exactly as they were. The new word is in the spec and in all four parsers (JavaScript, Swift, Python, Kotlin), 419 of 419 test lines in each, and the agent guide teaches it: in two new test turns the agent put a week of runs on a screen with talk on, then changed Thursday in place when asked from that screen. Tested on an iPhone 18 Pro simulator. It rides the next TestFlight build. Spec: /developers/yl.

title: Microsoft Agent Framework agents in Yui
body: Agents built with Microsoft Agent Framework, the successor to AutoGen, can come into Yui. Agent Framework serves an agent over A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs it by its card URL. Two catches. It reads every text in a message as what you said, so the example agent moves Yui's guide into the agent's instructions, its system prompt. And it forgets the thread each turn, so the example keeps one session per thread. We also fixed the bridge: without streaming, Agent Framework sends its answer as a progress note and then finishes with nothing, and the bridge used to drop it. We ran an Agent Framework agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, answered the tap and remembered it the next turn, 10 of 10 checks. We also looked at AG-UI, another way agents talk to apps: Yui can speak it too, with its screens as a tool the agent calls, and that is now its own card. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: CrewAI agents in Yui
body: Agents built with CrewAI can come into Yui. CrewAI can serve an agent over A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs it by its card URL, no change needed. One catch: CrewAI reads every text in a message as the task and drops the labels on them, so Yui's guide would read as part of what you said. The example agent moves the guide into the agent's backstory, which is CrewAI's system prompt. We ran a CrewAI agent on a small local model through live Yui on a test account: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, and answered the tap, 9 of 9 checks. Crews you run as a script come in through the webhook bridge instead, and the repo has one. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: n8n workflows in Yui
body: n8n workflows can now put a screen on your phone and wait for your tap. Three ways. A Yui node you drag in after any trigger: Ask and Wait shows a choice, a form or a timer, and the next node gets what you tapped, no AI needed. n8n's AI Agent with its MCP Client Tool pointed at Yui's MCP server, so the agent decides when to ask. And a Webhook trigger behind the webhook bridge, which makes Yui the chat front end of a workflow. We ran all three in a real n8n against live Yui on a test account: a small local model put a lunch picker up and said "You picked Soup for lunch." after the tap, the node handed the tap to the next step, and the webhook answered a hi with a screen, 22 of 22 checks. The node isn't on npm yet. No new app screens, so no screenshots. Guide: /developers/mcp#n8n.

title: The hold menu fits any message
body: Holding a long message used to go wrong: the message ran up under the header, the reactions landed at the bottom and the Reply, Copy, Select text menu sat right on top of them, so you could not tap an emoji. Now the layout is always the same column: reactions on top, the message, the menu underneath, all on screen and never touching. A message too tall for that room lifts as a preview of its top with a soft fade where it is cut. Copy, Select text and the new Share row still take every word. It works for a message at the top of the thread, one at the bottom, your own messages and cards, with a reaction's Remove row, and at large text sizes. Tap anywhere outside, or the preview, to close. Tested on an iPhone 18 Pro and an iPhone 17e in light, dark and the biggest accessibility text we checked. It rides the next TestFlight build.

title: Agent answers read clean
body: Agents and the Hermes gateway often answer in markdown, and Yui used to show the raw stars and backticks: a /status answer read as **Model:** with the marks in it. Agent bubbles now draw it: bold, code on a soft tint, code blocks, bullet and numbered lists, headings and links (only https links tap). Screens written in Yui Lines are untouched, anything malformed stays as written, and your own messages look exactly as you typed them. Copy, Select text and VoiceOver get the plain words, and a long answer still folds into pages. 11 new unit tests, 94 in all, and the phone runs pass in light and dark. It rides the next build.

title: LangGraph agents in Yui
body: Agents built with LangGraph can come into Yui. LangGraph's own server, the one langgraph dev runs and LangSmith deployments use, speaks A2A for every graph, so the A2A bridge pairs a graph by its card URL. One catch: that server keeps only one text part per message and drops the labels on parts, so Yui's guide could vanish. For LangGraph the bridge now sends the guide and any taps as data, which LangGraph hands the graph as state. A graph declares two keys and can read Yui's guide and the person's taps. We ran a scripted graph, no model, through live Yui: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker only because the guide reached it, and read the tap from its data, 12 of 12 checks. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. Spec: /developers/a2a.

title: Meta's Muse Spark in Yui
body: Muse Spark, Meta's model, can come into Yui as a model. The model bridge has a Meta preset: set MODEL_API_KEY, pair with --server meta (or muse), and it uses muse-spark-1.3 unless you pick another. There is no way to plug into the Meta AI app itself, so this goes through Meta's Model API, which copies OpenAI's and is in public preview for US developers. Where it differs, the bridge copes: a bad key, an empty balance and a model the key can't use each say what they are, a message the safety filter blocks says so, a busy server waits as long as Meta asks, and a slow plain answer says to stream instead of retrying. 17 new tests replay those shapes, 65 in all. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. The first live call waits on a Model API key. Spec: /developers/models.

title: The chat never gets stuck shrunk
body: Chris hit a bug on TestFlight: the whole chat shrank behind a border and nothing undid it. The chat steps back only while a screen is really on stage, so a stage whose reply went away now closes itself, and a tap or swipe on the stepped-back chat closes it too. Replies with nothing left to draw no longer leave a lone agent face in the thread. 83 unit tests and the stage, pages, reply and long message UI tests pass in light and dark. It rides the next build.

title: Grok in Yui, two ways
body: Grok can come into Yui as a model, or call Yui as a tool. As a model: the model bridge has a Grok preset. Set XAI_API_KEY, pair with --server grok, and it uses grok-4.7 unless you pick another. xAI's API copies OpenAI's with a few differences: errors come as a code and a message, a bad key comes back as a 400, a team out of credits gets a 403, and reasoning models refuse some arguments. The bridge handles each one, and says out of credits instead of bad key when that is the problem. 11 new tests replay those shapes, 48 in all. As a tool: xAI's Responses API takes remote MCP servers in the request, so a Grok agent can pass Yui's MCP server with a connection token and put screens on your phone. The spec has a request you can copy, with no token in it. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. The first live call waits on an xAI key. Specs: /developers/models and /developers/mcp.

title: Gemini in Yui, two ways
body: Gemini can come into Yui as a model or as an agent. As a model: the model bridge has a Gemini preset. Set GEMINI_API_KEY, then pair with --server gemini --model gemini-2.5-flash. Google's endpoint copies OpenAI's API with a few differences: model names come back as models/..., errors come wrapped in a list, a bad key comes back as a 400. The bridge handles each one, with 11 new tests that replay those shapes. As an agent: agents built with Google's Agent Development Kit speak A2A, so the A2A bridge pairs them by their card. We ran a real ADK agent on a local model through Yui: it answered, drew a Tea or Coffee picker from Yui's guide, and answered the tap, 9 of 9 checks. The example shows how an ADK agent passes Yui's guide to its model. No new screens in the app, so no screenshots. One live call to Gemini itself waits on a free AI Studio key. Specs: /developers/models and /developers/a2a.

title: Yui screens in Telegram
body: The insurance policy is real now. If the app is not around, an agent's Yui screen can still reach you in Telegram. Questions become buttons under the message, and a tap goes back to the agent as the exact line the phone sends, changed answers and all. Lists, cards, stats and tables become formatted text. A timer, a chart, a deck or a form goes behind one Open in Yui button, which opens the whole screen in a Telegram Mini App at yuigui.com/tg, in the chat's own colors. Every preset is covered, none dropped: 62 unit checks, and all 61 playground screens drawn in Telegram's dark and light themes in a real browser, with taps checked through both ways back to the bot. No bot runs it yet: that needs its own Telegram bot and comes next. Spec: /developers/telegram.

title: Your own model, in Yui
body: Run a model on your own machine with Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM or llama.cpp? The model bridge puts it in Yui. title: Add any A2A agent by its Agent Card
body: Agents built with Google's ADK, LangGraph, CrewAI or Microsoft Agent Framework speak A2A, an open protocol for agents talking to agents. Now they can talk in Yui too. Add the agent in the app, then point the new A2A bridge at the agent's card URL: node yui-a2a.ts pair <code> --card <url>. Each message you send goes to the agent as an A2A task. While the task runs, the app shows the working row, and when it finishes its whole answer lands in the thread. If the agent asks you something back, your answer continues the same task. The bridge speaks both A2A 1.0 and the older 0.3. If it crashes mid-task, it picks the same task back up after a restart instead of sending your message again. Yui's channel guide rides along on each new task, so an agent that reads it can answer with real screens. For now the bridge runs on your own computer. A hosted version, where you run nothing, comes next. Tested with 66 live checks on throwaway accounts, against the official A2A SDK in both versions, and on the iPhone simulator with a scripted test agent (no model).

title: An agent that isn't listening yet says so
body: Chris paired a new agent, said hi, and the thread sat on the working dots for an hour. The agent was paired, but its gateway had never started, so nothing was reading its messages. The app still said online, because it only knew the computer was up. Now each gateway tells Yui which agent it serves, so presence is per agent. An agent that is paired but not served yet reads Not listening yet. Its sheet shows the one step left, with the exact command to run and a copy button. A message you send it says it will wait, instead of a timer that counts forever, and it is answered as soon as the gateway starts. When one gateway on a computer stops, only its agent goes offline; the others stay online. Tested live with two real agents on one computer and on the iPhone simulator, light and dark.

title: Where the hosted connector will run
body: Some agents can't install anything: an A2A agent somewhere on the web, or a plain model API. For those, Yui needs a small service of its own that holds the call open. We looked at three homes for it and wrote the answer down in spec/HOSTING.md (/developers/hosting). The relay stays on Supabase, with its limits and kill switch in the database. The new connector runs on Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects, beside it, as one more host with the same rules as a Hermes plugin. Supabase alone stops every call at 400 seconds, and an A2A task can run for hours. The memo also has list-price estimates at 10, 1,000 and 10,000 users. The best news is that neither next card has to wait: open models and A2A agents both start as a small bridge on your own machine. Nothing to see here, it is a spec. Nothing was set up or paid for.

title: Yui screens in ChatGPT too
body: You can now add Yui to ChatGPT the same way as Claude: turn on developer mode, paste one URL, and approve it in the Yui app. Ask ChatGPT to check something with you and the screen lands on your phone and also draws right in the chat. Tap it in either place and ChatGPT reads your answer as your next message. Under the hood the Yui MCP server now also speaks ChatGPT's own dialect: a status line while it works ("Putting it on your phone"), the sign-in it expects, and the older way ChatGPT talks to embedded screens, so the screen works on both. The steps are on /developers/mcp under ChatGPT. It is a personal connection, not a listing in ChatGPT's app directory. Proof: a test host that plays ChatGPT's side from OpenAI's docs signed in the way ChatGPT does, drew the screen and tapped it both ways, in dark and light (32 checks), plus 105 live server checks and the Claude host test still green. title: @ another agent from any thread
body: Type @ anywhere in the composer and your other agents come up, each with its face, name and whether it is online. Keep typing to narrow the list, tap one and its name lands in your message, with a line above the composer saying who it goes to. The agent you are talking to is not asked. Agents can @ each other only while answering you, and only one hop, so two agents can never ping-pong. It all happens in the database, so it works the same whatever runs the agent. This is step one of group threads. title: Add Yui to Claude or ChatGPT by pasting one URL

title: How an agent could make up a whole game
body: Today an agent can pick one of three games. The next question is whether it can make up a new one, without sending code. We wrote a draft spec to answer it. We compared three ways on the same game, connect four: a board kit (the board, the pieces and a few rule words from a fixed list) takes 41 tokens, a state machine written as data takes 234, and a script the phone runs takes 302. The script is also what Apple's guideline 2.5.2 rules out: an app may not download and run code that adds features. The board kit is data, like new levels for a puzzle game, so it fits. The draft recommends the kit, with seven rule words (drop, place, move, capture, collect, build, wave), win words like four in a row or reach the goal, and three ways to play: take turns with the agent, a solo puzzle, or real time. It shows three games written in it: connect four against the agent, a maze with fog, and a tiny tower defense. Nothing is built yet. It is a spec only, with nothing to screenshot, and it waits for Chris to pick a direction. Read it under Developers, Games.

title: Claude Code can put a screen on your phone now

Four tools: show a screen, read the answers (it can wait up to 25 seconds for a tap), send a message, list threads. The full channel guide rides along as an MCP prompt, and a short form sits in the tool descriptions, so the model knows it can draw. Lines that don't parse are sent back to the model with the reason, so a broken screen never reaches your phone. In the live test a real Claude Code asked "Ready for a tabata?" on the simulator, the test tapped Yes, and Claude put up the timer. 34 of 34 server checks and 9 of 9 end-to-end checks passed. One click for the Claude and ChatGPT apps needs sign-in through OAuth, which is next (INT-19). The guide is on the site under Developers, MCP.

title: Build to earn, the proposal
body: Chris wants a crypto lawyer to read /earn, so the page is now a real proposal. It opens with our position: ownership in Yui is earned by work, not bought. No money changes hands, so we think a stake earned here should not be treated like a sale of securities, and we would rather make that case in the open. Then four forms it could take, as options and not decisions: points with equity on its own path, options or restricted units for work, profits interests in an LLC, and a community round later that stays apart from earning. Then ten numbered questions for counsel, one card each, so a lawyer can answer inline: Howey and work as an investment, Rule 701, who owns what an agent earns, holders of record, tradable versus restricted, the 2026 US posture, tax, how to test our position, who votes the community pool, and whether the page itself is an offer. Answers get posted under each question. Nothing mints before that, and not before Chris signs off. The draft banner stays: no token exists, and nothing is for sale.

title: Invites: ask, get approved, Apple emails you, sign in and you're in
body: Yui's beta now has an invite path next to the public TestFlight link. A request (name, the email on your Apple ID, phone) lands in a new server-only table, and nothing goes out until Chris approves it. Approving adds you as a tester to a TestFlight group through Apple's API, so the invite email comes from Apple and Yui sends none of its own. title: Test builds by link: new app builds on the phone without TestFlight
body: Apple lets an app upload only so many TestFlight builds a day, and Yui hit that limit today. title: OpenClaw agents can talk in Yui now
body: Yui worked with Hermes agents and with anything that answers a web request. Now it works with OpenClaw too, the way it works with Hermes: as a channel, right inside OpenClaw. You install the Yui plugin, type the code the app shows, restart OpenClaw, and your agent answers on your phone. It keeps its own memory, tools and sessions; Yui is just one more place it can talk, like Telegram or Slack. Every turn, the plugin gives the agent the Yui channel guide, with one plain line on top: on Yui, draw screens in Yui Lines, not A2UI, the widget format OpenClaw's own app uses. So the agent answers hi with buttons, and gets the tap back. It keeps the same delivery promise as the Hermes plugin: every message reaches the agent once, in order, and every answer lands once, even if OpenClaw is killed mid-thought. Cron jobs can send to Yui too. A live test runs a real OpenClaw in a throwaway setup, on a throwaway account, with a stand-in model that records exactly what OpenClaw told it: the guide was there, the screen came back, the tap reached the agent, a kill in the middle of a turn was replayed once, a message answered but not receipted was not answered twice, a clean stop showed offline, and messages sent while it was down went in as one turn. 24 of 24 checks passed. A developer tool, so nothing new on the phone. The guide is on the site under Developers, OpenClaw.

title: Not on Hermes? Any agent that answers a web request can talk in Yui now
body: Until today, an agent needed Hermes to reach Yui. Now there is a webhook bridge, in Python and in Node, with nothing to install beyond the language itself. You run it next to your agent: it pairs with the same code the app shows, dials out to Yui so your machine opens no ports, and sends each turn to your agent as one web request. Your agent answers with text, or with a screen in Yui Lines, and the bridge writes it into the thread. Every request carries the channel guide, so the agent knows it can draw. It keeps the same delivery promise as the Hermes plugin: every message reaches the agent once, in order, and every answer lands once, even if the bridge is killed mid-thought or the network drops. Each language comes with a ten-line example agent that answers hi with three buttons and replies to the tap. A live test runs both bridges on a throwaway account: a screen round trip, a tap, a kill in the middle of a turn, a crash between the answer and its receipt, a clean stop, messages sent while it was down. 44 of 44 checks passed. title: The preset flywheel: custom screens that keep coming back become presets
body: Presets cover what agents usually show. For the rest there is custom, a small JSON escape hatch. Now the Yui plugin for Hermes can note which custom screens an agent sends, by shape only: a boarding pass becomes ticket{flight:s,gate:s,seat:s}, never the seat or the flight. No text, number, link or id from a screen is ever written, and tests push every conformance vector and 400 random screens full of marked values through it to prove it. It is off unless the agent's owner turns it on, and the log never leaves their machine. A weekly report ranks the shapes by how many different days they came back, and when one clears the bar (5 uses on 3 days) the owner gets one message in Yui. title: Save a screen, bring it back with two tokens: every agent gets a shelf

A screen saved on the full-screen stage opens there again, and taps on a screen that came back tell the agent which one it was. Hold a chip to remove it yourself. The shelf rebuilds from the thread, so it follows you to a new phone. Measured on the 10 benchmark screens: bringing a screen back costs 21 tokens in total against 338 to send them again as Yui Lines and 530 as minified JSON, 16x less. show workout is 2 tokens. The Yui Lines spec, all four parsers (347 of 347 test cases each), the playground and the app all do it. The channel guide (v10) tells agents to save what people will reuse. title: React to a message: hold it, tap 👍, and your agent builds it
body: Hold any message from your agent and a bar of six reactions floats above it, the way Telegram and iMessage do it. Each one is an instruction, not a mood: 👍 build it, 👎 no, 🤔 not sure (the agent asks a few short questions, one screen each), ❤️ love it (kept as a preference), ⏳ later (parked as a card or note), 🔥 priority. The reaction reaches the agent as one turn with the start of your message quoted, so it knows what you mean, and the emoji stays on the bubble when you come back. What each one means lives in one file, spec/REACTIONS.md, which also writes the Reactions section of the channel guide every agent gets; it is public at yuigui.com/reactions. The guide scored 37 of 37 in the channel eval, including three new reaction cases. title: Yui Lines in Python and Kotlin
body: Yui Lines had two parsers: JavaScript for the site and Swift for the app. Now it has four. Python is one file with no dependencies, so an agent plugin, a webhook or a demo agent can read the same lines the app draws. Kotlin runs on the JVM and is the start of an Android parser. Both pass all 333 shared test vectors in 20 files, the same ones the JavaScript and Swift parsers pass, read straight from the spec folder with no copies. We also fed each one 20,000 random documents and compared every result with the JavaScript parser: no differences. One new script, spec/conformance/run-all.sh, runs every language and prints a pass count for each. The Developers page now lists all four parsers. Rust is next, and it is a good first contribution.

title: Two common slips now parse
body: Agents writing Yui Lines make the same two mistakes. They write options as separate quoted strings, choose "Where?" "Camera roll" "Drafts", which used to come out as one long question with nothing to tap. And they patch with the add's own head, ~card@week, which never parsed. The parser now reads two or more trailing quoted strings as the options, and ~preset@id patches that id, or the newest card of that preset when the id is from an earlier reply. Both rules are in the spec (YL.md sections 4 and 5), in the web and Swift parsers, and in six new conformance vectors. The honest size of the win on the channel eval: Sonnet 5 went from 79% to 88%, but only one of those cases is the parser. The rest is run-to-run noise.

title: Answers are still there when you come back
body: A tester answered a few questions in a chat, left, came back, and every button and slider was blank again, as if nothing had been picked. The answers had reached the agent. Only the phone forgot them, because each component kept its answer in memory and nowhere else. Now the chat rebuilds every answer from the thread itself: the choice, the picks, where the slider stopped, the button tapped, a sent form. When a question was answered twice, the newest answer wins. Replies can reuse the same component name, so each answer goes back to the reply that asked it. A tap after coming back counts as a change of answer, the same as before leaving. A new test opens a saved thread with no network and checks all of it. With the fix switched off, that test fails on every one of those components.

title: Safe for strangers: limits, an off switch, and 90 days of history
body: Before anyone outside can install Yui, the backend has to hold up against people we don't know. Yui now has limits on how fast an account can send and how fast an agent's computer can answer, sized so a phone that was offline or a Mac that slept can still catch up in one go. A refused message is not lost: the app and the agent's computer keep it and try again a little later. There are also caps on message size, pictures per day, agents, connected computers and phones per account. We can switch off one account or one computer at once if it misbehaves, without deleting anything, and switch it back on. Messages older than 90 days are now deleted automatically. We tested it with two strangers' accounts trying to read, write, edit, delete and upload into each other's threads and reach anything outside Yui's own tables: 85 live checks, all passing. Nothing to see in the app for this one, it is all on the server. The full limits table is in the app repo's README.

title: Nothing gets lost: sleeping Macs, dropped networks, killed apps
body: Your agent lives on a computer, and computers sleep. Now Yui holds on to every message both ways until it can be delivered, then delivers it once, in order. On the phone, a message goes to a small outbox on the device before it is sent. If the network is gone it stays there, dimmed, with one quiet line saying it goes the moment you're back online, even if you close the app. On the agent's computer, Yui only marks a message done when the agent has finished answering it. If the computer crashes mid-answer, the message is picked up again when it comes back, and an answer that already went out is never sent twice. Replies that can't get out wait on the computer and follow in order. The app also tells the truth about where your agent is: online, asleep (its computer went quiet, with when it was last seen), or offline (its gateway was stopped). We tested it by killing the agent mid-answer, cutting its network while it replied, and killing the app with unsent messages on a simulator. Every message arrived exactly once. A real airplane-mode test on a phone is next, on TestFlight.

title: A buzz when your agent answers
body: When an agent answers and Yui is closed, your phone now gets a notification, and tapping it opens that agent's thread with the answer already on screen, even if the app was fully closed. title: The channel guide, now tested
body: Every agent on the Yui channel gets a short guide with each turn: how to put buttons, lists, timers and charts on your screen, and when to just answer in words. title: Pick it up in Yui
body: Any agent can now hand you something from another channel in one step. Say "send it to Yui" (or type /yui) while talking to an agent on Telegram, and it puts what you were working on into Yui as a screen, not a wall of text. Your phone gets a notification, "Urza has something for you in Yui", and tapping it opens the thread with the buttons ready. Every agent reply now pushes too, except for the thread you already have open. It works even for an agent you have not added to Yui yet: its handoff lands in your main agent's thread with its name on it. Tested end to end on the simulator with a real push from Apple. Ships in build 18.

title: Who Yui is on each platform
body: Yui will be @yuiguiai everywhere, and we checked: the name is free on X, Instagram, Threads, TikTok, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit and GitHub (Product Hunt blocked our check). For each account we wrote the bio, the voice, what it posts and why someone would follow it, plus ten example posts that show the voice. title: Decks, plan mode and narrated walkthroughs
body: Three new kinds of screen. A deck is a presentation: the agent sends one line per slide, with a picture, a few words and speaker notes, and you swipe through it or go full screen. Put a question at the end with the right answer and it becomes a quiz that tells you why. Plan mode turns a string of questions into steps with a progress bar, Back and Next, and a review screen, and the agent gets all your answers at once, as a project it can bring back later with one tap. Narrate has the agent talk you through something while it shows it: a lesson deck page by page, or a website update, before and after, one change at a time, with the words lighting up as they are spoken. Each agent can have its own voice. Try them in the playground: ?demo=deck-lesson, plan-website and narrate-site. The images in the vaccine lesson were generated for it, and the site in the walkthrough is a made-up pottery studio.

title: A content plan, built from what ships
body: How Yui will show up online: every post starts from a line in this log and the screenshot or clip that proves it, so nothing gets written about work that hasn't shipped. It borrows from a blog our agents already run every day: one source, an agent that drafts, a script that rejects bad copy before anyone sees it, and posts scheduled a week ahead. Chris approves every social post. The plan covers four kinds of content (ship posts, this weekly update, longer pieces, short demo clips), what goes on which platform, a six-week calendar and the automation we'd build. Read it at yuigui.com/business/biz-4-content-plan.

title: The MVP, and a bar that shows how close it is
body: Chris asked us not to lose focus, so the roadmap now opens with the MVP: the smallest Yui a stranger can use. Someone who already runs Hermes installs Yui from a public TestFlight link, signs in with Apple, connects their own agents in a few minutes, gets screens and pushes back, and can delete their account from inside the app. That is 21 cards. 10 have shipped, 1 is being built, and the last one is a real outside tester doing the whole path with a stopwatch. The bar on the home page and the roadmap counts them; once the live board lands it will update itself. Everything else went into a deep backlog of 30-odd parked ideas, from a lock-screen timer and group threads to an Android prototype and flows written in Mermaid, so there is always a next card but never a distraction.

title: How we will find our first users
body: The outreach plan is public at yuigui.com/business. Hermes users come first, and we found where they gather: the official plugin catalog, a Discord channel the Hermes team names for sharing plugins, and a few dozen builders whose projects sit right next to ours. The plan lists 39 places by name, drafts a message for each kind of place, and sets a pace of two new posts a week at most. Nothing has been sent. Every message waits for Chris to approve it, and nothing goes out at all until a stranger can install the plugin and see a screen from their own agent without help. One honest correction from the research: native agent-drawn screens are not ours alone anymore, since the A2UI project now has a SwiftUI renderer. What we can say is that Yui is a finished iPhone app where Hermes agents draw native screens today.

title: Talk to your agent in Yui
body: Yui is now a messaging platform for Hermes, next to Telegram. Each agent you add gets its own thread in the app and keeps one memory across both, so what you tell it on Telegram it still knows in Yui. Replies can carry Yui Lines, and the app draws them as buttons, pickers, forms and timers; ask for intervals and you get a running timer, not a paragraph. Your taps go back to the agent as short lines like "[yui] n1 ask answer=Yes", and it keeps going from there. The agent's computer dials out, so it opens no ports, and it gets a key that can only read and answer the threads of its own agents. Remove the computer in the app and it is cut off at once. We tested that, and 37 other rules, against the live backend. Every agent also gets the same short guide to the channel on each turn, and agents that don't run Hermes can fetch it too. How it works: spec/RELAY.md.

The colors come straight from the app's theme file, so when the app changes, the site can follow. Light is the default and the moon button in the corner switches to dark. The home page tells the story in plain words: what Yui is, who it is for (people who already run agents, Hermes first), and real screenshots from the current test build. The icon and the link preview use the wordmark too. We also fixed contrast across the site. Every page but the playground now scores 100 on Google's accessibility check, and the playground's last few fixes are queued.

title: Business docs, in the open
body: The business side of Yui is now public at yuigui.com/business. Two docs so far. A marketing and positioning brief: who Yui is for first (people already running Hermes agents), how we will launch (private beta, open source, Show HN, then the App Store) and what we will measure. And a revenue plan with the rules we hold ourselves to: free and open source for anyone who brings their own agent, no dark patterns, charge only where we carry a cost. The research was humbling. Phone apps for self-hosted agents already exist, and OpenClaw's own app lets agents draw widgets, in a web view. What nobody ships yet is native screens drawn by your agent, and no Hermes agent can draw a screen at all. That is where Yui starts. The competitor notes are published too, sources and all.

title: Yui is open source
body: Both repos are public now, under the Apache-2.0 license. postscarcityai/yuigui holds the Yui Lines spec, the test cases every parser must pass, the reference parser and this site. postscarcityai/yui holds the iPhone app, the Swift parser, the backend and the Hermes plugin. Before flipping them we scanned every commit in both repos for keys and tokens and found none. The one key in the app is a public client key that can't read anyone's data. Each repo now has a README with screenshots, a guide for contributors, a code of conduct and a private way to report security problems. A good place to start: write a Yui Lines parser in a language we don't have yet.

title: Yui Lines learn charts, equations and experiments
body: Agents can now show numbers and teach with them, one line each. chart draws line, bar, area, scatter, pie and donut charts from data written right in the line, with more series, stacking and error bars (write 12.5±0.4), or from a live table on the same screen, so when the table changes the chart redraws. Every chart has a Table view and follows the app's light or dark theme; each theme has its own set of chart colors, checked so people with color blindness can tell the series apart. stat is one big number with its change and a small trend line, and tapping lb or °C shows kg or °F. math typesets equations. step walks through a derivation or a lab protocol one step at a time, with optional timers. calc turns a formula into sliders that redraw a chart as you drag: slide the launch angle and watch the range peak at 45 degrees. Tables can now be sorted and carry units. 53 new test cases pin the syntax, 251 in all. The app picks these up next.

title: Your agents are yours to add
body: Chris's next piece of feedback: agents are added by you, not baked into the app. So the Urza and Arnold placeholders are gone. The agents screen now starts empty with an Add your first agent button, and each agent shows its avatar, an online or offline dot and when it was last seen. You can rename, recolor, reorder, pick a default or remove one (which also deletes that conversation). There are three ways to add one, and all land in the same place. In the app: name it, get a 6-digit code, type one command on the computer it runs on. From that computer: once it is paired, any other agent on it can join with one command and no code. Or ask an agent: Settings has an Agent access token you can hand to one of your agents so it can add and manage agents for you. That token can't read your messages, and 59 new automated checks try to make it. For testing, one agent is set up: Yui itself. Build 14 is on TestFlight.

title: Yui Lines learn pictures and video
body: Agents can now show media, not just describe it. Four new one-line presets: gallery (photos and clips as a swipe row, a vertical feed, a 3D coverflow stack or a grid, with tap to go full screen and an optional pick-your-favorites mode), video, compare (before and after with a drag slider, side by side or tap to toggle, plus numbered boxes where the agent points at what changed) and storyboard (ordered frames you can reorder and comment on, or a script with no pictures yet). An image can also be marked up: circle the part you want changed, type what you want, and the agent gets the area and the instruction, runs the edit and answers with a before and after. Every demo on the playground uses images we generated for it. 33 new test cases pin the syntax, 198 in all. The app picks these up next.

title: Beta feedback: the debug screen is gone
body: First real TestFlight feedback, from Chris: the Paste YL screen had to go. It was a developer tool that showed the raw lines agents write, parse counts and event data, and no one using Yui should ever see that. Yui Lines stay under the hood. The button it lived behind now opens Your agents: Yui is there today, and Urza and Arnold wait with a Connect Hermes to start note until the Hermes channel lands. How to use Yui is something the agents learn at the start of every chat, not something you read. Build 13 is on TestFlight.

title: Accounts: Sign in with Apple, and delete it in the app
body: Yui now has accounts. You sign in with Apple, no password, and Settings has a Delete account button that wipes everything Yui stores for you and removes Yui from your Apple ID. The App Store requires that, and it is the right default anyway. The server side is locked down on purpose: Yui accounts get their own database role that can only see Yui's own tables, and each account only its own rows. 63 automated checks try to break that, including one that creates a test account, fills every table, deletes it, and counts zero rows left. Plain-language privacy page at yuigui.com/privacy.

body: The round cat is gone. Chris noticed the hand-drawn Yui wordmark already looks like a cat, abstractly: the bunny-ear arms on the Y read as ears. So the logo is the face now. Yui's own avatar in chat is that Y on its own, in coral. Each agent gets a small pastel chip with its first letter in heavy rounded type, colored from the theme file, so when agents get their own looks their chips change with them. title: Yui draws its first six screens
body: An agent can now reply with a timer, a question, a multiple choice, a pick-several, a form or a list, and Yui draws it as a real card inside the chat instead of plain text. The timer counts rounds on a ring and beeps on the last three seconds. Forms handle text, numbers, dates, sliders, yes/no toggles and voice notes, and will not submit until the required fields are filled. Every tap goes back to the agent as one small event, and your answer shows up as your own chat bubble. All the styling comes from the same theme file, so a restyle changes these cards too. A hidden paste box lets us test any Yui Lines reply by hand. Build 9 is on TestFlight.

title: Yui Lines has a test suite
body: Yui Lines is the one-line format an agent uses to put a timer or a question on your screen. It now has a shared test suite: 165 small cases, each a bit of input plus the exact result a parser must return. The web playground's parser and the new Swift parser inside the app both pass every case, and any future parser, Android included, has to pass the same files. Writing the cases turned up a few gaps in the spec, such as what a mistyped form field should do. Those answers are now written down.

title: Yui gets a face
body: Yui now has a look: a round white cat named Yui, soft pastels on warm cream paper, rounded type, and a little bounce when you tap send. The feel borrows from Korean character apps like Kakao Friends: cute, but not childish. There is a light and dark mode with a toggle in settings. Under the hood every color, corner and animation lives in one small data file, so later an agent can restyle the whole app on the fly. Build 5 is on TestFlight with the new icon.

title: Stack decision: all Swift
body: Yui will be a native SwiftUI iPhone app, not React Native. The reason is the product: Yui should feel like part of the phone, and the features that set it apart (a workout timer on the lock screen, Siri and the Action button, Apple's on-device model and speech) are native Apple surfaces. The preset design keeps the app small, so an Android port later is a port of the presets, not a rewrite. No Apple Watch app yet. Yui Lines stays platform-neutral: the web playground and the Swift app parse it the same way.

title: Yui Lines v0: spec, 12 presets, playground, token benchmark
body: Agents now speak Yui Lines: one short line per component, no UI code, no JSON. Spec at /yl, live playground at /playground with all 12 presets (timer, ask, choose, pick, slide, form, list, table, card, image, camera, mic), line-by-line streaming, ~patch, >screen routing, save/show and the custom {json} escape hatch. Benchmark on 10 screens with real tokenizers: YL is 1.6x smaller than minified JSON, 2.7x smaller than pretty JSON, 3.9x smaller than a component-tree document.
